# 1.

# WELL SUMMARY

## 1.1

EXPLORATION, EVALUATION AND OPERATION SUMMARY

PL 103, Block 25/7 was awarded to the Conoco - Britoil Norge/BP Norway - Amerada Hess - Statoil group in 1985 and the first well, 25/7-1, was drilled in 1986. Well 25/7-2, situated in the SE part of the block, was spudded on February 8, 1990, with the semi-submersible drilling rig "Dyvi Stena". The well location is approximately 5.3km SW of the 25/7-1 location.

Block 25/7 is situated in the southern part of the Viking Graben (Fig. 1.2). The block is bounded to the east by the Utsira Basement High. The well was designed to test for the presence and the hydrocarbon potential of Upper Jurassic submarine fan sands derived from the Utsira High. Secondary objectives were sands of Middle Jurassic age.

Gas readings were generally low down to the Draupne Formation with values approaching 0.15% total gas. Relatively high gas readings were seen while drilling the Jurassic section with trip gases reaching 10% in the coal beds of the Sleipner Formation.

Oil shows were first observed in the lower part of the Draupne Formation. The Top Upper Jurassic Conglomerate and Sand Formation was penetrated at 4119m MD. Four cores were cut from 4125m-4169m MD. Oil shows were present in the cores and described as dull yellow fluorescence, instant clouding blue white cut fluorescence and pale yellow white residual fluorescence.

One core was cut in the Hugin Formation 4461.5m-4488m MD where none to weak shows, very dull golden brown fluorescence, very slow clouding cut fluorescence, yellow white residual fluorescence were described. No oil shows were seen below 4550m MD.

A total of 49 RFT pressure tests were taken in the Upper Jurassic Conglomerate and Sand Formation and the Hugin Formation. It was not possible to establish a hydrocarbon/water contact based on the RFT measurements.

Three intervals; 4148m-4173m, 4193m-4218m and 4248m-4273m in the Upper Jurassic Conglomerate and Sand section were perforated and drillstem tested. The well flowed at maximum rates; of 9030 mmscfg/d and 1435 bblsc/d, through a 40/64" choke, but both the pressure and rates declined rapidly during the test period.

The well reached a total depth of 4852m MD in rocks of Middle Jurassic age in 131 days from spud and 142 days from taking over the rig. A further 29 days were used to log, test, plug and abandon the well.

Well 25/7-2 was plugged and abandoned at 07:00 hrs on the 18th of July 1990. The rig was on contract for a total of 171 days.

# 2.2 COMMUNICATIONS AND LOGISTICS SUMMARY

All operations were coordinated from Conoco Norway Inc.'s facilities at Dusavik. Norsea
Base in Dusavik provided all pipe yard space as well as drill water, potable water, and
bulk cement and barite. Fuel was purchased from Norske Shell's facilities in Tananger.

Transportation in support of 25/7-2 was a multi-faceted operation. Personnel movement
to and from the rig was provided by Aerospatiale Super Puma helicopters. The
helicopters, operated by Helikopter Service, flew out of Sola Airport in Stavanger.
Round trip flying time was approximately 2 hours, with three scheduled flights per
week. Additional flights were easily arranged when needed to maintain drilling
operations. Equipment and material movements to and from the rig were provided for
by two AHTS vessels. Combined capacities of these vessels included:

| No. | Capacity | Description |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 1. | 893 m2 | cargo deck area |
| 2. | 1,428 m3 | fuel |
| 3. | 2,500 m3 | fresh water/drill water |
| 4. | 21,500 ft3 | bulk cement/barite |
| 5. | 2,068 m3 | oil spill recovery |

Communications with the Dyvi Stena were excellent. Written messages were transmitted
via telefax. Verbal communication and computer data transfers were performed via a
satellite telephone system.

# 3.1.2 Conclusions and Recommendations

MOBILIZATION, ANCHOR AND R/U

Four days were estimated for this operation. Approximately ten days were actually used.
This was due to waiting on weather (6.6 days) and problems with setting anchor no.
1. A piggy back anchor was run on anchor no. 1. (A total of seven days and sixteen and
a half hours).

It is recommended for future rig contracts to specify that the rig has at least 17.5 ton
anchors (Stevins for instance). With a better anchor, the no. 1 anchor might not have
slipped. Small LWT anchors should be avoided. The weather down time is almost
unavoidable at this time of year as this is a very weather sensitive operation.

36" HOLE/30" CASING

Two and a half days were estimated on this hole section to drill 17 1/2" hole, open to
36" and run and cement 30" casing. Three days and twenty hours were actually used.

The anomalies identified as possible shallow gas indicators at 205m and 250m MD by
the site survey were never observed. Due to possible shallow gas a 17 1/2" pilot hole
was drilled and then opened with a 36" HO. As the hole opening assembly was pulled
out of the hole, it was discovered that all welds on the four 10" square tubes around the
30" housing receptacle on the Dril-Quip PGB were cracked. The PGB had been landed
and secured to the moon pool trolley, allowing the forces of the waves to transmit a
considerable momentum directly onto the PGB welds. The PGB should have been set
on a narrow solid frame. The Dyvi Stena had no system to hang off the PGB/30" casing
assembly.

26" HOLE/20" CASING/BOP AND RISER

Five days and six hours were estimated to drill the 17 1/2" pilot hole, open to 26", log,
run and cement 20" casing. Two days were estimated to run the BOP and riser.

The actual time used was seven days and nine hours on 26" hole/20" casing and nine
days and thirteen hours were used to run BOP/riser.

a) 26" Hole/20" Casing

As the site survey data indicated possible shallow gas, a 17 1/2" pilot hole was
drilled riserless and then opened to 26". The estimated shallow gas zone at 295m
was never observed.

# a) Claystone Group

Because of the chemical and mechanical instability of this interval, an inhibitive fluid
with adequate mud weight is required to drill this section successfully. In order to ensure
and minimize problems related to sloughing of the borehole, good hole cleaning
practices are imperative. Adequate flow rates, optimum mud rheology, and controlled
ROP will alleviate problems related to excessive cuttings in the wellbore.

While drilling at 1938m, the torque increased suddenly and the hole packed off. The
pipe was worked free and full circulation regained. The torque increase was not due to
bore restrictions but rather to build up of cavings in the hole. When reaming out of the
hole, heavy cuttings returns were seen.

Problems with mud pump no. 2 at 1920m (drive chain broke) reduced the annular
velocities below critical limits for the transport of the cavings.

Nut plug pills were pumped at 1940m to clean the bit. The torque went up from 5500
ftlbs to 12000 ftlbs, but dropped back to 5500 ftlbs.

On several occasions, following a trip, the roller cone assembly became packed off with
dry, hard cuttings when tripping back to bottom. This problem was probably the result
of jamming the bit into the cuttings accumulated at the bottom of the hole, thereby
packing off or balling the bit. This problem was successfully alleviated with the use of
fresh water pills to disperse the reactive clay polids.

This is the Heimdal through Ekofisk interval consisting of normally pressured sandstones with clay and lime intervals.

Problems such as partial mudlosses and stuck pipe were experienced in the Heimdal sand. The partial mud losses were solved by pumping an LCM pill.

The string packed off and became stuck with the bit at 2378m when pulling out of the hole to change bit. Due to this, it is recommended to use the top trip and backream, and pump in and out of the hole through the Heimdal sand.

Overbalance should be limited to allow formation face cleaning below the bit, and to prevent filtercake build up in the porous zones. As in the previous interval bit hydraulics should be optimized.

Bits with gauge protection should be run in this interval to avoid undergauge hole and to allow drillstring weight and torque to reach the cutting structure, rather than being expended at the stabilizer. Three out of the four bits used in this interval were graded undergauge when pulled.

At 2747m the drillstring twisted off in the lower service threads on the Dailey jar while drilling. The jars were in slight tension with 65-70000 lbs WOB. However, problems with bit bouncing might have led to the jar being both in compression and tension. High bit weight of 70000 lbs used together with 100-130 RPM resulted in the least bouncing and the highest ROP.

Fifty eight and a half hours were used on fishing operations caused by the parting of the jar. It was found that the jar had been used in a fishing job without inspecting the internal threads prior to sending it back offshore.

# BITS DISCUSSION

The drilling assemblies were of packed BHA design using a 9 1/2" Nortrak Mach-I-P/HF positive displacement motor, designed to give higher torque and flowrate, and slightly less RPM. Fixed cutter PDC bits were used.

The three types of bits that were used were of similar design. They all had medium taper - shallow cone profile, and had ribbed hydraulics design with changeable jets. They employed medium sized cutters and, other than bit no. 13 (LX301), a heavy cutter setting density.

Bit no. 13 was a Diamant Boart LX 301 which drilled the 13 3/8" casing float equipment and one hundred and sixty six meters of limestone (Kyrre and Trygvasson formation, 2974m - 3140m). The average ROP was 6.4 m/hr. The bit grading is presented in the bit record.

Bit no. 14 was an EC Z437G. Three hundred meters of limestone which graded into argillaceous limes and calcareous claystones were drilled with this bit. The run terminated at the base of a 40m sand section (Trygvasson and Blodøks formation, 3140m - 3440m). The average ROP was 3.87 m/hr. The bit was pulled due to mud motor failure. The most significant wear element was the nose ring-out. This failure was completely radial at a circumference just outside the nozzle array. It appeared that one cutter was lost causing the ring out into the bit matrix.

Bit no. 15 was a Diamant Boart LX-401 and was used to drill 149m of calcareous claystone and interbedded limestone stringers (Blodøks and Svarte formation, 3440m - 3589m). The average ROP was 2.67m/hr. The bit was pulled due to low ROP. The most significant wear point was on the nose.

Bit no. 16 was an EC Z437G. The formation drilled was predominately claystone with limestone interbeds in the uppper part (Svarte and Rødby formation, 3589m - 3914m).

In well 25/7-1, thirteen bits were used to drill the 12 1/4" section. The 13 3/8" casing and the 9 5/8" casing were set higher on 25/7-1. Comparing the bit runs in the same formations such as Kyrre, Trygvasson and Blodøks, 6 bits were used on 25/7-1 (3.29 m/hr) and 2 bits were used on 25/7-2 (4.5 m/hr).

In general, the use of PDC bits and mud motors was a good choice. Bit trips were drastically reduced, and the ROP's were higher than experienced on 25/7-1 where rockbits/insert bits were used.

It must be remembered that a different mud system was used on 25/7-2. There is still room for improvement in bit selection on future wells. Also, greater care must be taken while running in hole to prevent stuffing of bits into fill on bottom without circulating and rotating. This may prevent some of the bit balling experienced.

# 8 1/2" HOLE

The 8 1/2" hole was drilled from 3900m to 4850m through the lower part of Cromer Knoll, and the Upper and Middle Jurassic.

The interval from 3900m to 4350m was rotary drilled using two bits (EC Z437GN and S225). The average ROP was 2.38 m/hr.

The remaining interval was drilled with a Neyrfor turbine, and five bits of type TBT703 (Diamant Boart), H223 (Hycalog), S226 (Eastman Christensen), H223 (Hycalog),and T51 (Eastman Christensen) were used. The average ROP on the turbine runs were 3.19 m/hr.

The turbine and the thermally stable diamond bit combination worked very well compared to offset bit records. An economical analysis done by D.M.Hejnal (IOC, Turbine performance-25/7-2) showed a cost saving 212,000 USD. Attributable to the use of turbines in this interval.

The final two bit runs were discounted from this comparison due to:

1) significant difference in geology.
2) a different turbine and bit type used on the last run.

Recommendation: The turbodrill/diamond bit combination is recommended for the 8 1/2" hole. Recognize that the cuttings generated are extremely small.

Problems encountered in this hole section were:

A) Two incidents of stuck pipe.
B) Logging problems.
C) Corebarrel jamming.
D) Metal wear on tool joints and 9 5/8" casing.
E) Turbine failure

A) At 4306m, the pipe got stuck with the bit at 4304m (Claystone) while making a connection. The pipe came free by jarring and circulating at 600 GPM. Time lost due to stuck pipe was two hrs.

While making a connection at 4345m, the drillstring got differentially stuck at the 6 1/2" drillcollars in the permeable sand between 4250m and 4295m. The differential sticking should not have been a surprise at this point after being stuck previously at 4306m. Very close attention was being paid to pore pressure detection, and previous mud weight increases followed increases in formation gas. The sticking at 4306m should have been a warning that the well was significantly overbalanced, and that additional mud weight increases should have been avoided.

The Neyrfor 7 1/4" T3A1 turbine was laid down with severe wear on the lower

A 6 5/8" turbine was run in the hole and drilled to TD at 4850m where the tool
failed. The turbine deterioration after only twenty four and a half hours was
interpreted as a result of the extra bearing wear induced by the off bottom
reaming at maximum flowrate.

During turbine drilling operations, the mud rheology began climbing, and
additions of chemicals could not stop the increase. The problem, in fact, was a
fine solids build-up problem, and could have been minimized by running the
centrifuge at all times. This is very important in turbodrilling applications since
the fine cutting structure turning at 500+ RPM produces very small, finely
ground cuttings which are not removed with the primary equipment (shale
shakers). As the ultrafine cuttings are recirculated, they are further reduced in
size due to the shear of the surface equipment and bit. The requirement for
expensive high temperature conditioning polymers is increased if the ultrafine
solids removal is not optimized. This can only be achieved with the fulltime use
of the centrifuge system.

# 3.2    DRILL STEM TESTING SUMMARY

A single drill stem test was conducted over the hydrocarbon bearing interval of the
Upper Jurassic sandstones. The main objectives of the test were:

- * To ascertain the types of hydrocarbon present.

- * To see if the well could flow at commercial rates.

- * To evaluate the near well bore area by pressure
  transient analysis.

A total of 75m was perforated with 4 1/2" wireline conveyed guns in six 12 1/2m runs.
Gun specifications were: 5 shots per foot at 60 deg phasing, 37 grm HMX charges. The
perforated intervals of the well were:

4148 - 4173m
4194 - 4219m
4248 - 4273m

After perforating a junk basket/gauge ring was run to the top of the DST interval. A
wireline set permanent packer was then set at 4130m.

The DST string was run with a full cushion of drill water to surface, which gave an
underbalance of 3800 psi. A high underbalance was run to give the interval a chance
to clean up mud from the perforations and to expel any solids from drilling the interval.

The PCT was opened for an initial flow period at 1325 hours, 10 July 1990 through a
24/64" adjustable choke. The initial flow period lasted 6 minutes. An estimated 20 bbls
of cushion was unloaded during the initial flow.

The well was then shut in downhole for initial build up which lasted 59 minutes.

A main flow period of 15 hours and 55 minutes was conducted through a 40/64" fixed
choke. Gas came to surface after 25 minutes and flow was diverted to the separator
after seven hours and 23 minutes.

The final flowing wellhead pressure was 1287 psia at 102ºF. Final flow rates were
8.085 mmscf/d of gas, 886 bbls/d of condensate and 17.2 bbls/d of water.

The well was then shut in downhole for 31 hours and 3 minutes for the main build up.
Downhole pressure increased from the final flowing pressure of 2774 psia to 7070 psia

# 3.3  PLUG AND ABANDON SUMMARY

The plug and abandonment process commenced on 13 July 1990. An EZSV packer was set at 4127m, and 20 bbls of 16.0 ppg mud were injected into the perforations from 4148m to 4273m. This was followed by four cement plugs set in the intervals from 4273m to 4107m, 3844m to 3789m, 3789m to 3713m, and from 395m to 195m.

The 7" tie-back string was perforated at 181m with a 1 11/16" 4 shot perf gun, cut at 177m and retrieved. The 9 5/8" casing was perforated at 171m and then cut at 168m before being recovered. The 13 3/8" casing was perforated at 161m on the second attempt (faulty detonator tube), cut and pulled together with the 18 3/4" x 13 3/8" hanger. The BOP and riser were then pulled and secured. The 20"/30" casing strings were cut 6m below the mudline at 155m and pulled with the PGB. A 5" cement stinger was rih to 176m, and the top hole section and crater was filled with 137 sxs class "G" cement with 25% silica. The ROV performed a final seabed survey of the wellsite and surrounding area.

Anchor handling commenced at 1420 hours on 17 July 1990 with the final anchor bolstered at 0642 hours on 18 July. The anchor handling was interrupted for 7.5 hours to change out the Cameron connector on the BOP to a Vetco H-4 connector. The Dyvi Stena left the 25/7-2 location at 0700 hours with the Viking Troll in the bridle. Total time spent on the plug and abandonment process was 4 days and 17 hours.

# SUMMARY OF EVENTS  
## 36" HOLE SECTION: CONOCO NORWAY INC. 25/7 - 2

Prior to spud in, 1900 bbls of mud were mixed. These consisted of 750 bbls of kill mud at 12.0 ppg (weighted PHB/SW mud), 650 bbls of prehydrated bentonite at 40 ppb, and 500 bbls of prehydrated bentonite/seawater fluid blended in a ratio of 3:2, giving a funnel viscosity of around 40 secs/quart. Extra volume for this section was subsequently mixed in a similar manner.

The well was spudded at 0445 hrs on 04/02/90, a 17 1/2" pilot hole drilled from 149m (RKB to seabed depth) to 265m using seawater pumped at 28 bbls/min, returns to the seabed. ROP averaged 25 m/hr. 30 bbl hi-vis sweeps were pumped around the hole every 10 metres and prior to each connection. The sweeps were made from the prehydrated bentonite / seawater fluid flocculated with lime prior to pumping, to give a final funnel viscosity of 60 - 80 secs/quart. At 265m a 50 bbl pill was circulated around, then 100 bbls were displaced to the hole prior to pulling out for the hole opening assembly.

The pilot hole was then opened to 36", drilling with seawater pumped at 28 bbls/min to a depth of 259m. 50 bbl.high viscosity sweeps ( made as previously ) were pumped every 10m and prior to connections. ROP averaged 29 m/hr. A 100 bbl hi-vis pill was pumped around the hole prior to a wiper trip at 259m, and upon returning to bottom a similar volume of spud mud was circulated around before displacing the hole with 600 bbls of 10.0 ppg mud. This was made by blending appropriate volumes of 12.0 ppg kill mud and unweighted PHB/SW fluid. Whilst the casing was run and cemented the kill mud volume was rebuilt to 805 bbls at 12.0 ppg. Cement was displaced with seawater.

A total of 4737 bbls were built during this section: 2308 bbls were used, leaving 2429 for use in the next section. This 2429 bbls consisted of: 1071 bbls of prehydrated bentonite (40 ppb), 805 bbls of 12.0 ppg kill mud, and 553 bbls of prehydrated bentonite / seawater fluid ( 3:2 ratio ). Daily usage is recorded in the volume summary section.

The chemical costs for this section were NOK 117206. This calculates at NOK 24.74 per barrel, and NOK 1010.4 per metre drilled. This latter figure includes both pilot hole and the opening of the hole within the price. The section took 2 days (from spud in to casing cemented).

# SUMMARY OF EVENTS

## 26" HOLE SECTION: CONOCO NORWAY INC. 25/7 - 2.

2429 bbls of mud were left from the previous section for use during this phase. Further spud mud was mixed as required by prehydrating bentonite at 40 ppb in fresh water, and cutting the mixture with the required amount of seawater. For high viscosity pills this was done in the ratio of 3 parts PHB to 2 parts seawater, which was then flocculated with lime prior to pumping; for weighted fluid the ratio was 1:1 to give 20 ppb bentonite in the fluid prior to barite additions.

Cement was drilled from 252.5m to 259m, and a 17 1/2" pilot hole was drilled to 1030m. Seawater was used, pumped at 28 bbls per minute, returns to the seabed. ROP varied between 30 and 200 m/hr. 50 bbl high viscosity pills were pumped around the hole prior to each connection, and at 1030m a 200 bbl hi-vis pill was circulated and 75 bbls of 12.0 ppg mud spotted on bottom prior to a wiper trip. After the trip a further 200 bbls of hi-vis spud mud were pumped, followed by 800 bbls of 10.0 ppg mud being displaced to the hole. The well was then logged and drilling continued, 100 bbls of spud mud pumped prior to each connection. A twist off occured at 1053m: a 100 bbl high viscosity pill was circulated around the hole and 10.0 ppg mud was spotted on bottom prior to pulling out. The fish was successfully retrieved and the pilot hole was drilled to 1218m, pills pumped as before. At 1218m, a 200 bbl sweep was pumped prior to spotting a further 200 bbls of 12.0 ppg fluid in the hole prior to pulling the string.

The hole was opened to 26" pumping seawater at 27 bbls per minute, 100 bbl pills pumped around the hole every 10m. 2m of new hole were drilled to 1220m. ROP averaged 25 m/hr, up to a maximum of 45 m/hr. 2000 bbls of hi-vis mud were spotted on bottom prior to the wiper trip, and upon return to bottom a 500 bbl sweep was pumped around prior to spotting 1800 bbls of fluid at 10 ppg followed by 700 bbls at 11 ppg in the hole. XCD polymer mixed in seawater was used in conjunction with prehydrated bentonite in the preparation of this mud, since the space on board was insufficient to prehydrate bentonite for the whole mix.

A further 1382 bbls of PHB/SW mud were mixed and retained on board whilst the casing was run and cemented at 1211m. This and all other remaining surface volume was dumped after the cement job was successfully completed, and mixing for the next section commenced.

A total of 13770 bbls of mud were built during this section; 2429 bbls were left over from the 36" section; 14607 bbls were used in the 26" phase, and 1592 bbls were dumped. Daily usage is recorded in the volume summary section.

# SUMMARY OF EVENTS

## 17 1/2" HOLE SECTION: CONOCO NORWAY INC. 25/7 - 2

Prior to the start of drilling the 17 1/2" section, a total of ten
days were spent preparing to drill, waiting on weather and
conducting BOP repairs. During this time 2622 bbls of mud were
mixed: 2062 bbls of 10.0 ppg fluid to displace to the active
system, 460 bbls of unweighted premix, and 100 bbls of prehydrated
bentonite at 25 ppb for a high viscosity sweep prior to displacing
the hole. The mud for the active system contained the following:
0.8 ppb Potassium Carbonate, 7 ppb KCL, 0.5 ppb XCD polymer, 0.5
ppb Drispac Superlo, 1 ppb Drispac Regular and 1.25 ppb PHPA. The
premix contained: 0.5 ppb Potassium Carbonate, 0.75 ppb XCD
polymer and 20 ppb WBS 200. This was sheared, using the rig pumps
through the shearing line, until the temperature exceeded 40
degrees Centigrade.

The shakers were dressed with DX 84 and DX 38 screens, 38's on the
front two sections of shakers 2 and 3, and 84's on the remainder.
This proved to be too fine a mesh for the initial drilling, and
the screens were subsequently changed to DX 24's on all 4 shakers
to minimise mud losses in this area.

Cement was drilled with seawater to 1220m, then a 100 bbl high
viscosity bentonite pill was circulated around the hole to carry
out any excess cement cuttungs, followed by 80 bbls of drillwater
as a spacer. The well was then displaced to 10.0 ppg mud: some 200
bbls were lost upon return due to a newly installed dump valve
from the gumbo box inadvertently being left open. A leak off test
was taken giving a 13.1 ppg equivalent mud weight.

From the start of circulation with the newly displaced mud, severe
losses over the shakers delayed drilling whilst new volume was
mixed to maintain active pit levels; these losses also
necessitated the screens being changed to DX 24 mesh. At around
1900m, these were staged up to three shakers with DX50 and one
with DX 84, and as the section progressed all screens were dressed
with DX 84 screens ( circa 2150m ) and finally DX 110 by 2725m.
When the 84's were being utilised, temporary replacement with DX
50's on the middle two shakers was necessary during bottoms up
after trips to minimise losses, but once the 110's were installed
this was no longer required. With the exception of bottoms up
volumes, where contaminated mud was allowed to flow over the
screens, shaker losses were generally kept to a minimum from 1900m
onwards.

Driiling of 17 1/2" hole commenced at a controlled drilling rate
of approximately 30 m/hr. A reserve volume of 1400 bbls of mud
was prepared and weighted to 10.0 ppg. This contained the
following: 0.25 ppb Potassium Carbonate, 0.75 ppb XCD polymer, 1.6
ppb Drispac Superlo and 13ppb KCL. This was to be used for
supplementary volume maintenance (in addition to the premix
additions) and also to assist in retaining the desired level of.

At the shoe the mud weight of the system was raised to 11.6 ppg, the string pulled to 1165m and backreamed to 510m, where it was finally possible to pull out of the hole. The stabilisers were found to be totally balled up with very dry, hard shale. This further indicated that the hole problems encountered were not due to hydration and swelling of the formation, but to insufficient mud density and poor hole cleaning. The hole was reamed from 1210m to 1713m, adding 25 bbls per hour of reserve mud and 35 to 40 bbls per hour of premix (with 13 ppb WBS 200 and 0.5 ppb XCD polymer). An extra 0.25 ppb of XCD polymer was added to the system to improve the hole cleaning abilities of the mud. Once again an excessive volume of cavings came out of the hole. A trip was then made to the shoe and the string hung off due to bad weather, and upon running in again reaming was necessary from 1606m to 1938m. Premix containing 11 ppb WBS 200 and 0.5 ppb XCD polymer was added at 25 bbls per hour at this time. An 80 bbl high viscosity pill was pumped around the hole and the mud weight raised to 11.8 ppg. Once this conditioning was complete, an unsuccessful attempt was then made to drill, progress still being only 2m after a 30 bbl pill with 20 ppb nutplug had been pumped in an effort to clean a possibly balled bit. A trip was made, backreaming still required. The next bit run was no more successful, after reaming the bottom 67m of the hole the bit would not drill, and was found to be balled with very hard shale cuttings. On the next run in the hole, reaming was necessary from 1572m to 1940m. The mud was heavily conditioned, 1085 bbls ( 40% of the active system ) being dumped and replaced with new reserve volume, thus injecting a large dosage of fresh chemical into the system. This was necessary due to the bacterial degradation of the polymers, as indicated by the foul smell of the mud returns and loss of rheology and filtrate control. The entire system was thus also treated with 500 ppm Ancocide, (Gluteraldehyde bactericide), and all existing and new reserve and premix volume built thereafter was treated with a similar dosage.

Drilling then continued at an average of 5m per hour to 2005m, treatment consisting of premix additions at 11 to 20 bbls per hour, the premix now containing 16 ppb WBS 200 and 0.8 ppb XCD polymer. A further 10 bbls per hour of weighted reserve mud was also added to the active. A bit trip was made at 2005m, and the hole was reamed from 1570m to TD. Whilst drilling to 2130m several drill water pills were displaced around the bit and allowed to soak for some minutes in efforts to alleviate bit balling, this being reasonably successful. ROP averaged 6m per hour through this limestone/claystone formation. At 2130m a trip was made and the riser was displaced to seawater in preparation for hanging off due to adverse weather conditions. Meanwhile the gumbo box, header boxes and sand traps were dumped and cleaned out. Upon resumption of drilling, some 200 bbls of bottoms up mud was allowed to flow over the shakers since it was heavily contaminated with fine drill solids. It was noted however, that there were considerably less cavings and sloughings than previous trips.

3622 bbls of mud at 13.8 ppg were left over from the 12 1/4" phase for use in this section. The shakerboxes and sandtraps had been dumped and cleaned after the 9 5/8" cement job. 739 bbls of contaminated mud were dumped from pit 1, and the pit then thoroughly cleaned.

Cement was drilled from 3883m to the shoe, the rathole and formation drilled to 3917m, and a leak off test taken giving a 17.9 ppg equivalent mud weight. The active was treated with 10 bbls per hour premix, consisting of the following: 3.2 ppb Ancolig, 2.2 ppb Drispac Superlo, 3 ppb Anco Resin and 1.75 ppb WBS 200. Further Anco Resin was also added direct to the system. The mud weight was raised to 14.0 ppg at 3920m.

Shakers were initially dressed with a combination of HP200, DX210, and DX175 mesh screens. Shaker number 2 was redressed with DX110 mesh screens to allow barite to pass through efficiently and thus provide the geologists with a better formation sample. Later in the section all shakers were dressed with DX210 and HP200 screens, a combination that was retained for the remainder of the drilling of the 8 1/2" hole. These adequately handled the flow, with occasional losses due to excessive foaming. It was not felt that changing the screen size would have curtailed these losses.

8 1/2" hole was drilled through claystone formation to 4079m, the density being raised in stages to 16.0 ppg. These were; 14.2 ppg at 1450m, 14.7 ppg at 3962m, 15.2 ppg at 4000m, and 15.6 ppg at 4006m. Simultaneously the system was treated for thermal stability with additions of Hostadrill, Narlex, Anco Resin and Ancolig. Premix containing these products was also added continuously to the system, at rates ranging from 5 - 20 bbls per hour. Concentrations in the premix were generally maintained as follows: 3 ppb Ancolig, 1 ppb Hostadrill, 2 ppb Narlex and 4 ppb Anco Resin. Centrifuges were usually run at all times whilst circulating, liquid discharge from centrifuge 3 being returned to the active or dumped via pit 2 as volumes and mud condition dictated.

A variety of defoamers and combinations of defoamers were pilot tested, and the better results applied to the active system, including the use of peanut oil, which, in addition to it's lubricative properties, tended to assist in curbing the foam as well.

# 3.12 PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION

## WELL 25/7-2 PORE PRESSURE SUMMARY

Pore pressure prediction in the 25/7-2 well was difficult due to varying sequences of
sand, shale and limestone throughout the well. Rock bits, mud motors, PDC bits and
turbines that were used during the drilling phase did not appear to hamper pore
pressure detection techniques with the exception of shale cuttings density when the
turbine was used. Parameters used to determine pore pressure and transition zones
worked at various times. Drilled formation pressures were difficult to determine though
using the various parameters.

The pore pressures presented hereafter are subject to interpretation. All that can
actually be said about the pore pressures is that they were below mud weight that was
carried throughout the well. One exception is in the 17-1/2" section. Hole problems
were eliminated when the mud weight was raised indicating a near or underbalance
situation. DST and RFT data closely follow the pore pressure curve in the Upper
Jurassic formation and this was the only pressure data obtained during the drilling of
the well. Following is a brief discussion concerning the pore pressure parameters used
during drilling of the well.

### Shale Cuttings Density

Measured shale cuttings densities were from 0.3 to 1.0 gm/cc lower than bulk density
log measurements. The lower shale density readings obtained by the mud loggers could
be a result of inconsistent drying of cuttings, contaminated fluid used to measure
densities or inconsistent selection of cuttings size for measurement. Fluid used to
measure the shale density may have been a contributing factor. Neothane and zinc
bromide are used in the fluid column instead of neothane and tetra bromoform. This
is a result of tetra bromoform being banned from use in the Norwegian North Sea due
to its classification as a carcinogen. There have been reports that the zinc bromide and
neothane mixture yields invalid measurements but this has not been verified. As a
result, the shale cuttings densities were viewed quantitatively for shifts in trend lines.

### Resistivity

The MWD and electric log resistivities appeared to be valid through the 9-5/8" casing
point. Both the MWD and E-log resistivities indicated pressure transition zones. Below
the 9-5/8" casing point, the resistivity measurements were considered erroneous. MWD
and E-log resistivity measurements did not tie in with measurements obtained through
the 9-5/8" casing point. The measured resistivity measurements may be a result of
different formation but did not correspond with established trends in the upper part of
the well. The resistivity trend line below the 9-5/8" casing point did not correspond
with density or sonic trends.

- 158 -

AI.page_summary: Summary of pore pressure evaluation for well 25/7-2: pore pressures were generally below circulating mud weight, with an exception near the 17-1/2" section. Shale cuttings density measurements were 0.3–1.0 g/cc lower than log densities, potentially biased by fluid choice (zinc bromide/neothane). MWD and electric resistivity were reliable above the 9-5/8" casing but became inconsistent below it; DST and RFT supported Upper Jurassic pressure curve.

OCR.ocr_markdown:
# E-log Density

Log derived density measurements indicated transition zones and areas of higher than
normal pore pressure. As is true with other log derived pore pressure detection
parameters, transition zones and abnormal pressure zones are determined after the well
section has been drilled. Density measurements appeared to work well with regards to
pore pressure detection.

# E-log Sonic

Log derived sonic interval transit times also indicated transition zones and high pore
pressure zones. The higher than normal pore pressure zones and transition zones
indicated by the sonic measurements correlate with the density derived measurements
and other detection parameters. Sonic measurements appeared to work well with
regards to pore pressure detection.

# Rate of Penetration

Bit rate of penetration was successful in various degrees in determining high pore
pressure areas. More often than not, increased ROP was mistaken for increasing pore
pressure when in reality the ROP increased due to a change in formation. This
misinterpretation led to unnecessary increases in mud weight.

# Gas Measurements

Background and connection gas was used to detect increasing pore pressure. Attempts
were made to keep background gas reading at 5% or less. When connection gas or
background gas exceeded 5%, the mud weight was usually increased as the gas readings
was used to indicate increasing pore pressure. Some of the drilled formations contained
more gas than others. The increased gas readings were mistaken for pressure instead
of zones that contained gas that were normally pressured or contained a pressure less
than the mud weight that was used to drill the formation. Mud weight should not have
been increased until more formation had been drilled to determine if the gas readings
were a result of localized gaseous formations or pressure was in fact increasing. In most
instances the mud weight was increased almost immediately to reduce the gas readings.

# Temperature

MWD and mud in/out temperature plots were used throughout the well. The
temperature plots indicated pressure transition zones but did not qualitatively yield the
pressure. The temperature plots were viewed with a "grain of salt" below 4340 mRKB
as a turbine was used to drill the remainder of the well. The use of a turbine will
increase the temperature of the mud in/out and MWD temperatures. This affect can be
seen on the MWD temperature plot after the turbine was placed in the well.

Notes that density and sonic logs correlate for detecting transition and high pore pressure zones; ROP can be misinterpreted; gas spikes often led to premature mud weight increases; turbine use affects temperature plots below 4340 mRKB.

# D Exponent

The modified D exponent yielded the best indication of drilled pressures. A trend line
shift for the D exponent occurred at +3260 meters. When the trend line was shifted,
it was not parallel to the original trend line which resulted in higher pressures being
calculated from the D exponent than were actually drilled. The shifted trend line was
redone to ensure that it was parallel to the original trend line and calculated pore
pressures using the D exponent were within 0.06 sg (0.5 ppg) of DST and RFT pore
pressures. Care must be exercised to ensure that trend line shifts are parallel to original
trend lines.

## Pore Pressure Discussion By Hole Interval

### 26" Hole Section

The 26" hole section was drilled from the 30" shoe at 259 mRKB to 1218 mRKB with
the 20" casing shoe being set at 1210.5 mRKB. Seawater was used to drill this hole
interval. Pore pressure appeared to be normal to +1150 mRKB. Pore pressure then
increased to an estimated value of 1.22 sg (10.2 ppg EMW) at 1218 mRKB. This
pressure increase occurred in the Miocene age formation. The 20" shoe leak off test at
1210.5 mRKB was 1.57 sg (13.1 ppg EMW). Estimated overburden gradient at this
depth was calculated to be 1.87 sg (15.6 ppg EMW).

### 17-1/2" Hole Section

This hole section was drilled to a depth of 2974 mRKB. Drilled formations were mainly
shales with minor sand stringers to the top of the Heimdal formation at +2250 mRKB.
The Heimdal is basically sand with some shale stringers present. Limestone was
encountered at 2924.5 mRKB or the Kyrre formation. The casing shoe was set in this
limestone formation. The pore pressure at the 20" shoe reversed almost immediately to
a normal pressure of 1.03 sg (8.6 ppg EMW). At approximately 1330 mRKB the pore
pressure appeared to increase relatively quickly to 1.2 sg (10 ppg EMW) at +1400
mRKB. Pore pressure calculations indicate that the drilled pressures fluctuated between
2l0 (9.8 ppg EMW) to 1.38 sg (11.5 ppg EMW) from 1400 to 2000 mRKB. The
pressure peaks above 11 ppg EMW occurred in this interval. Mud weight used to drill
these peaks was 1.30 sg (10.8 ppg). The drilled hole was sticky on trips with excessive
cuttings seen on shale shakers. At +1900 mRKB the mud weight was increased to 1.32
sg (11.0 ppg EMW) and was again increased to 1.42 sg (11.8 ppg at +1935 mRKB).
Hole problems with regard to cuttings amount and stickiness all but disappeared after
the mud weight was increased.

Pore pressure decreased from 1.22 sg (10.2 ppg EMW) to normal at +2250 mRKB. This
pore pressure reversal was expected as it occurred in the Balder and Heimdal
formations. The Heimdal formation is a massive sand section with large areal extent.
Faults presumably do not exist in this formation which eliminates potential traps to trap
pressure. Pore pressure increased from normal at +2700 mRKB (top Ekofisk) to

# 4.    GEOLOGY AND GEOPHYSICS

## 4.1    GEOLOGICAL SETTING

Block 25/7 is situated in the southern part of the Viking Graben, approximately 180 km west of the Norwegian coast (Fig. 4.1.1).

The block is bounded to the east by the Utsira Basement High, and a system of predominantly north-south major boundary faults. These fault systems delineate the eastern part of the Viking Graben. The East Shetland Platform/Fladen Spur is bounded by similar north-south trending faults which represent the western Viking Graben boundary.

Structurally, block 25/7 is analogous to the Brae Field area along the western flank of the Viking Graben.

The 25/7-2 prospect is located on the downthrown side of the major north-south boundary fault. The location is 5.3km southwest of 25/7-1 which failed to test the Upper Jurassic sandstones. 25/7-1 drilled into basement after the Cretaceous section without penetrating any Jurassic sediments. With the 25/7-2 location further to the west one expected to penetrate a complete Brae analogous sequence (Fig. 4.1.2).

## 4.2    OBJECTIVES AND RESULTS

Well 25/7-2 was drilled to serve as the second of two commitment wells on block 25/7, in accordance with the PL 103 License Agreement. The well was planned to be drilled to a total depth of 4875m (RKB), 120m into the Middle Jurassic sequence. Main objectives were to test the development of Upper Jurassic sandstones and their hydrocarbon potential. Secondary objectives were sands of Middle Jurassic and Paleocene age.

The well successfully tested the geological model and encountered hydrocarbons in the Upper and Middle Jurassic reservoir sections. The well was tested and produced gas and condensate at sub-commercial rates. Figure 4.2.1 is a lithostratigraphic summary showing lithology and formation tops encountered in well 25/7-2.

# 4.6 WELL VELOCITY SURVEY

The 25/7-2 well seismic data were acquired and processed by Schlumberger for the
purpose of calibrating the sonic log and generating a synthetic seismogram and a
vertical seismic profile. The fixed source was a 500 cu. in. airgun positioned 50m from
the wellbore at a depth of 3.5m. The data were acquired in the cased hole using a
standard 3-component tool. A total of 161 levels were recorded between 500m and
4857m RKB. Of these, 138 levels below 2110m RKB provided usable data at 20m
intervals and were used in subsequent processing. Full details are available in
Schlumberger's "25/7-2 Sonic Calibration Processing Report" and "25/7-2 Vertical
Seismic Profile Processing Report", both issued Sep. 1990.

## 4.6.1 Sonic and Density Logs

The individual sonic logs were edited to remove noise spikes and casing effects, then
combined to form a continuous record. No sonic was recorded for 984-1196m RMSL,
due to the necessity to drill ahead out of sand to set casing deeper than planned. A
second gap in the sonic occurred at 2928-2943m RMSL due to bad bottom hole
conditions. The two gaps have been straight-line interpolated and treated as part of the
continuous sonic. The calibrated sonic log is contained in the Schlumberger report
listed above.

The density logs have been similarly edited and combined, with small gaps being
replaced with synthetic density curves. Spurious density values above 1184m RMSL
resulting from bad hole conditions have been edited out and replaced with a straight
line.

## 4.6.2 Synthetic Seismogram

The synthetic seismogram (GEOGRAM) was generated from the calibrated sonic and
density logs, using minimum and zero phase 35Hz Ricker wavelets. The resulting
synthetic traces are displayed in Figure 4.6.1, with the final displays contained in
Schlumberger's Sonic Calibration report, above.

## 4.6.3 Vertical Seismic Profile

The vertical seismic profile consists of 138 levels recorded between 2110m-4857m RKB
in cased hole using Schlumberger's 3-component Seismic Acquisition Tool (SAT). Levels
tested above 2110m RKB contained no useful signal, presumably due to casing effects.
Standard VSP wavefield separation and processing techniques were used to generate a
final upgoing P-wave (Z-axis) VSP, the corridor stack of which is shown in Figure 4.6.1.
Three-component processing resulted in isolating a down-going shear wavefield with
a prominent diffraction event interpreted to indicate a major disconformity
approximately 1.5 km from the wellbore. Intermediate displays and a final composite

# 4.8    FORMATION PRESSURE

## 4.8.1    Formation Pore Pressure

Pore pressure prediction in well 25/7-2 was difficult due to varying sequences of sand, shale and limestones throughout the well. Rock bits, mud motors, PDC bits and turbines that were used during drilling did not hamper pore pressure detection techniques with the exception of shale cuttings density when turbine was used. Estimation of pore pressure was measured by using shale cuttings density, resistivity logs, density logs, sonic logs, rate of penetration, gas measurements, temperature and the D-exponent. In the following, pore pressure is discussed by hole interval, and figure 4.8.1 summarises the pore pressure distribution in well 25/7-2.

The 26" hole section was normally pressured to ± 1150m MD. Pore pressure then increased to an estimated value of 1.22 sg (10.2 ppg EMW), at 1218m MD.

The 17 1/2" hole section was drilled to 2974m MD. The pore pressure at the 20" shoe reversed to normal 1.03 sg (8.6 ppg EMW) almost immediately. At 1330m MD the pore pressure increased to 1.2 sg (10 ppg EMW) and the fluctuated between 1.20 sg (9.8 ppg EMW) and 1.38 sg (11.5 ppg EMW) from 1400-2000m MD. Three pore pressure peaks above 11 ppg EMW occurred in this interval. Mud weight used to drill this interval was 1.30 sg (10.8 ppg EMW). The drilled hole was sticky on trips with excessive cuttings seen on shale shakers. When mud weight was raised to 1.42 sg (11.8 ppg EMW) at 1935m MD, hole problems disappeared.

Pore pressure decreased to normal at ± 2250m MD, before increasing again at ± 2700m MD in the Ekofisk Fm. Pore pressure at the 13 3/8" shoe was calculated to 1.16 sg (9.7 ppg EMW).

The 12 1/4" section was drilled to 3920m MD. The pore pressure build gradually over this interval to the top of the Lower Cretaceous. The estimated pore pressure at 3920m MD was 1.57 sg (13.1 ppg EMW).

The 8 1/2" section was drilled to 4850m MD which was TD. Drilled pressures increased from 1.57 sg (13.1 ppg EMW) to 1.63 sg (13.6 ppg EMW) at ± 4293m MD (Top Heather Fm.). A sharp transition zone was experienced in the Heather Fm. where drilled pressures increased to a maximum of 1.85 sg (15.4 ppg EMW) at the top of the Heather Sand Fm. Calculated drilled pressure reversed towards the bottom of the Heather Sand Fm. to ± 14.9 ppg EMW before increasing to 1.85 sg (15.4 ppg EMW) at TD, 4850m MD.

A trend shift on the D-exponent occurred at 3260m MD. Gas readings and calculated D-exponent pressures indicated a drilled pressure of ± 1.92 sg (± 16 ppg EMW) and mud weight was increased to 1.98 sg (16.5 ppg EMW) at 4320m MD. While making a connection at 4345m MD the drill string became stuck. The D-exponent was re-evaluated and it was found that the shifted trend line was not parallel to the original trend line. # 4.9.3    Stratigraphy

## 4.9.3.1    Quaternary - Uppermost Tertiary

**Nordland Gp. (149-883m MD)**

Returns to seabed, no lithology descriptions.

Age: Early Miocene to Pleistocene.

**Utsira Fm. (445.5-883m MD)**

Returns to seabed, no lithology descriptions.

Age: Middle - Late Miocene.

## 4.9.3.2    Tertiary

**Hordaland Gp. (883-2098m MD)**

Cuttings from 1210.5m MD. Only MWD from 1030-1185m MD. The group consists of brownish grey, firm, non calcareous, slightly dolomitic/ankeritic claystone, which becomes slightly micropyrictic and micro micaceous towards the base. The diverse benthic faunae and presence of planktonic forams imply deposition in an outer marginal marine environment.

Age: Eocene to Early Miocene.

**Rogaland Gp. (2098-2698m MD)**

Dominant lithologies in the Rogaland Group are sandstones (Heimdal and Ty Fm.) interbedded with shales (Sele and Lista Fm.). The sandstones pass laterally into shales westward. The uppermost formation of the group (Balder Fm.) consists of tuffaceous shales whereas the basal parts frequently contains reworked limestones and marls. The Rogaland Group was deposited in a relatively deep marine environment characterized by submarine fans which built out from the west, and possibly from the southeast.

Age: Paleocene - Early Eocene.

Varicoloured, predominantly greenish and brownish grey, tuffaceous, hard, laminated in parts, silty in parts, non calcareous, dolomitic, claystone. Traces of limestone and dolomite, off white, light brown, soft to hard. The formation was deposited in an inner to outer marginal marine environment.

Age: Late Paleocene.

## Sele Fm. (2184.5-2258m MD)

The formation consists of multicoloured, hard, amorphous to laminated, occasionally silty, dolomitic, sideritic, pyritic and micromicaceous claystone, interbedded with sand. The sand consist basicly of quartz, fine to medium, well sorted, subrounded to rounded. The formation was deposited in a nearshore environement.

Age: Late Paleocene.

## Lista Fm. (2258-2318m MD)

The formation consists of interbedded claystone, siltstone, sandstone and thin limestone/stringers. See below for more detailed descriptions.

## Heimdal Fm. (2318-2470m MD)

The formation consists of sandstone with interbedded claystone and occasional limestones. The sandstones are translucent, friable, fine to medium grained, sub angular, sub spherical, calcite cemented, and pyritic. The claystones are green, medium to dark grey, firm, laminated, pyritic and sideritic. The limestones are white, chalky, soft and micritic. The Heimdal Formation was most likely deposited in an outer marginal marine environment.

Age: Late Paleocene.

The dolomite is light brown, very hard, blocky, cryptocrystalline. The deposition of the Lista Fm. took place in relatively deep water under low energy conditions. The Åsgård Fm. consists of claystone, calcareous claystone (marl), limestone stringers and traces of siltstone. # Viking Gp. (4056-4407m MD)

The Viking Gp. in well 25/7-2 consists of shales with varying organic content and coarse clastics ranging from fine to medium sands to conglomerates. The Viking Group sequence seen in the well has no analogue elsewhere on the Norwegian shelf, but one good analogue in the British sector is found in the Brae area. The lower parts of the group were probably deposited in an open marine transgressive shelf environment. Increasing fault activity to the east changed the regime to a fault scarp submarine setting. The uppermost formation (Draupne) was deposited in a marine environment with anoxic bottom conditions.

Age: ?Callovian - Ryazanian

## Draupne Fm. (4056-4119m MD)

The formation consists of dark grey-brown to black claystone, non to slightly calcareous, carbonaceous, subsilice, traces of pyrite, with thin limestone stringers off white, very light grey, grayish brown buff, soft to moderately hard, blocky, with streaks and specks of argillaceous material, locally very argillaceous. The Draupne Fm. was deposited in a marine environment with restricted bottom circulations and often with anaerobic conditions.

Age: L. Kimmeridgian to Ryazanian.

### Upper Jurassic Conglomerates and Sandstones (Brae Fm. equivalent) (4119-4293m MD)

The formation comprises stacked conglomerates with beds of massive sandstones and minor thin beds of laminated shales in the upper part. Downwards the lithology changes to interbedded sandstones and claystones. The conglomerate is very poorly sorted, polymit, grading to breccia. The matrix grades from muddy sand to sandy mud. The Conglomerate beds range from clast supported to matrix supported. The clast lithology is both sandstone and claystone of varying age, their size grade from granules to big boulders, and are angular to rounded in shape. Frequently Belemnites are found, many beds show strong soft sediment deformation. The sandstones are light grey, grey to white, clear, quartz, fine to medium, massive, poorly to moderately sorted, subangular to subrounded, calcareous to silica cemented. The shale is dark grey to black, firm to hard, laminated, silty, micro-micaceous, pyritic. The vertical arrangements of facies and structural setting indicate that the conglomerates represents cohesive debris flows, the sandstones high density turbidities deposited in a fault-scarp submarine environment. Deposition by slumps and slides also took place.

Age: Oxfordian - Kimmeridgian

## Hugin Fm. (4407-4613m MD)

The formation comprises sandstones with minor claystone/shale and siltstone beds. The formation is generally getting finer grained towards the top. The formation consists of light brown grey to yellow, fine to medium grained sandstones, shale and coal. The sandstones are fairly sorted and the grains are subangular to subrounded. The sandstones are often bioturbated, calcareous or glauconitic. The formation was deposited in a near shore, shallow marine environment with occasional influence of continental fluviodeltaic conditions.

# 4.10  BURIAL HISTORY AND SOURCE ROCK MATURITY

## 4.10.1  Burial History

Sedimentation through Mid-Late Jurassic was characterized by alternating predominantly sandy and predominantly shaly layers. The thickness indicates an average sedimentation rate of ca. 3.7 cm per 1000 years. Water depth varied between 30 and 100m as reflected by the dominant grain size deposited. The top of the Jurassic is marked by an unconformity. It is difficult to estimate the amount of uplift and erosion associated with the unconformity. 100m of Late Jurassic - Early Cretaceous erosion is estimated. Because the main source rock for hydrocarbons is the Late Jurassic Draupne Formation, timing of hydrocarbon generation is not sensitive to the amount of erosion. The erosional episode was followed by a hiatus that lasted until Barremian. Sea-level rose throughout Cretaceous, interrupted by a short drop during Cenomanian. The Cretaceous sediments comprise a mixture of shale and carbonate. Fairly clean limestones were deposited during Santonian to Campanian. The sediment accumulation rate (2.4cm per 1000 years) decreased compared to the Jurassic time. Biostratigraphic data indicate a hiatus close to top Cretaceous. The hiatus is modelled to span 4 m.y. and coincides with a drop in sea-level. Sea-level rose again in Early Tertiary, then it gradually decreased until Mid Miocene before it rose to todays level.

Apart from the Late Paleocene, sedimentation throughout Tertiary was dominated by clastics. Sediments deposited during the Late Paleocene are similar to those deposited throughout Cretaceous i.e. a mixture of carbonates and shale. The thickness indicates average sedimentation rate of 4.3 cm per 1000 years. An erosional episode is modelled in Pleistocene.

## 4.10.2  Source Rock Maturity

Geochemical analysis of well 25/7-2, carried out by Geolab Nor (see separate report), indicates that the top of the oil generation zone is somewhere around 3200m RKB. The oil generation zone ends around 4200m RKB, and gas generation begins around 4600m RKB. The Draupne Fm., samples from 4060 to 4108m RKB, had initially a rich potential for generating oil. The Heather Formation, samples from 4293m RKB to 4665m RKB, initially had some, but variable potential for generating oil and gas. At present time the Draupne Formation is within the oil generation zone, but has passed the peak oil generation stage. The Heather Formation is within the condensate generation zone.

The condensate, discovered in the Upper Jurassic sandstone is sourced from the Draupne Fm. However, geochemical parameters seem to indicate that the source for the condensate is more mature than the Draupne Fm. penetrated in the well.

# Oil shows

Oil shows were first observed in sandstone stringers in the Draupne Formation below 4110m MD. It had a orange dull golden fluorecence, occasionally traces of very slow streaming clouding blue white cut fluorescence. No residual fluorecence.

In the cored section from 4125m to 4169m MD, a dull brown fluorence, instantaneous streaming clouding blue white cut fluorecence, yellow white residual fluorence was seen in the upper part. The basal part had occasional brown dull golden fluorecence, blue white streaming, very poor cut fluorecence and a yellow white residual fluorecence.

● Upper Jurassic Sand (Core 1-4)

### Description

The cored interval comprises mainly stacked conglomerates with some in situ beds of massive and parallel laminated sandstones and minor thin beds of in situ laminated shales.

Conglomerate: Dominantly very poorly sorted, polymict conglomerates grading into breccia. The matrix grades from muddy sand to matrix supported. The clasts varies from granules to big boulders and are from very angular to rounded. The clast lithologies are both sandstone and mudstone of predominantly Triassic, Middle Jurassic and possibly Late Jurassic age. Among them, a big clast of most likely Middle Jurassic age comprising interbedded sand and shale with a seat-earth and overlying coal. It is recognized as a clast by the fact that it is upside down. Frequently, Belemnites is found in conglomerate beds. There is no indications of internal structuring like imbrication, and only in a few cases can normal grading within beds be observed. Many beds shows strong soft sediment deformation.

Sandstone: In the cores it comprises units of stacked fine to medium grained sandstones, which internally shows massive bedding and some parallel lamination. There is also indications of water escape structures.

Shale: Laminated dark grey to black with some sandy/silty laminae and occasionally comprising belemnites.

### Depositional Environment

From the vertical arrangement of facies, and the depositional setting proximal on the down thrown side of the major fault, the conglomerates represent cohesive debris flows

## Heather Formation (Core 5)

### Description

Dark grey to blackish mottled, pyritic, bioturbated mudstone containing Belemnites. There is no visible lamination.

### Depositional Environment

Open marine mudstone deposited by hemipelagic settling from suspension.

## Hugin Formation (Core 6)

### Description

Dominantly very fine to fine grained, occasionally medium grained, medium to light grey, occasionally olive grey, intensely bioturbated, pyritic and micaceous sandstone. The bioturbation is generally so intense that classification of burrows is difficult; however, they seem to be mainly horizontal and some can be classified as Chondrites. In general a high mud content (10-20%) incorporated into the sand by bioturbation. Bed boundaries are generally difficult to define, however, they can be distinguished by increased mud content. Beds displaying sharp bases and parallel and massive bedding are occasionally seen. The sand comprises abundant shell lags, Belemnites and wood fragments.

### Depositional Environment

Transgressive offshore bars on a shallow marine shelf below the fair weather wave base. The sand transport mechanism to the depositional site was most likely by storms. However, most primary sedimentary structures were destroyed by sediment feeding organisms during low energy periods.
